cues.en: Every spring, I make my middle school history students record an interview with an older relative.
I expected nothing different from Olivia, a quiet girl who sat in the back row.
She handed me two unmarked discs.
Late that night in my study, I put the first disc into the player.
On screen, Olivia sat inside a cluttered living room across from her Great Uncle Stephen.
The old veteran smoked in silence, clutching a stack of yellowed papers.
When Olivia asked about his worst memory from the army, Stephen set his cigarette down.
He had been deployed to the Balkans after a brutal conflict.
His unit was sent to clear an old elementary school that had been obliterated years before.
The roof had collapsed, rain poured through cracked concrete, and no child had stepped inside for seasons.
In the flooded basement, Stephen discovered a handwritten letter left beside a heavy transistor radio.
It was written by Stanislav, the school's former janitor.
Stanislav wrote that after an illness took his wife and child, his radio was the only sound that kept him alive.
Grief had shattered his mind.
He returned to the destroyed schoolhouse every morning with his mop and broom.
He wrote that the teachers smiled at him in the halls, and the children enjoyed the low music from his radio.
He swept around broken desks, carefully polishing the rubble and moving aside whatever lay in the shadows.
Until one morning, the radio went dead.
Unable to bear the suffocating silence, Stanislav wedged a chair beneath the basement door and took his own life.
His note had one dying plea: Please fix my radio.
On the second disc, Olivia asked her uncle the question that still haunts me.
How could the janitor die in an empty school destroyed years earlier?
Stephen answered with a trembling voice.
The letter was dated only two weeks before their arrival.
Stanislav had spent two years sweeping a tomb, smiling at figures frozen in the dark, thinking the silence was alive.
And when Stephen finally forced the basement door open, the janitor was gone.
Sitting in the pool of stagnant water was the radio.
And in the dead silence, it was softly humming.
